title: Earth in Space
bigQuestion: What patterns in the sky can we see and measure, and what do they tell us about Earth's place in space?

story.title: The Shadow Stick on the Blacktop
story.kicker: A broom handle, a piece of chalk and one school day are enough to catch the Earth turning.
paragraphs: At 8:30 in the morning, Ms. Ortiz's class carried a bucket of sand and a broom handle out to the blacktop. They stood the handle straight up in the bucket. The sun was low in the east. The shadow of the stick stretched long across the pavement, pointing west. Devon traced its tip in chalk and wrote the time.

Every hour a different student ran out to mark it. By 10:30 the shadow had swung toward the northwest and gotten shorter. At 12:30 it was the shortest of the day. It pointed straight north, at the flagpole. By 2:30 it was growing again, sliding toward the northeast. The chalk marks made a curve.

Back inside, Devon had a question. 'The stick never moved. The bucket never moved. So what moved?' Half the class said the sun moved across the sky. The other half remembered something about the Earth spinning. Ms. Ortiz did not answer. She asked them to think about a merry-go-round.

When you spin on a merry-go-round, the playground seems to sweep past you. The slide, the fence, the trees all go by. But they are standing still. You are the one turning. Devon got it first. 'We are on the merry-go-round. The sun is the tree.' The sun only seems to travel. Earth is turning under it.

The next week they did it again, and the curve had shifted a little. The noon shadow was a bit shorter. The days were getting longer. Something else was changing, more slowly than the daily spin. This chapter follows those chalk marks: the day, the year, the moon and the stars, all from a stick in a bucket.
story.think: The shortest shadow of the day pointed north, toward the flagpole. Where in the sky was the sun at that moment?

lessons.title: Our Star, the Sun
lessons.mainIdea: The sun is a star like the ones at night; it looks huge and bright only because it is so much closer.
reading: The sun is a *star*. That may sound odd, because it does not look like the tiny sparks in the night sky. But it is the same kind of thing. It is a giant ball of hot gas that makes its own light. The night stars are suns too, unimaginably far away.

The sun is close, as stars go. It is about 93 million miles from Earth. Light is the fastest thing there is, and it still takes about 8 minutes to make the trip. When you feel sunlight on your face, it left the sun 8 minutes ago.

The sun is also enormous. About 109 Earths could line up across its middle. It looks small because it is far away, the way a jet looks like a speck when it is miles up. Never look straight at the sun. Its light is strong enough to hurt your eyes for good.

words.d: a giant ball of hot gas in space that makes its own light and heat
how far apart two things are

look.title: The Flashlight Down the Hall
look.text: Two identical flashlights are turned on in a dark hallway. One is held 3 feet from you. The other is carried all the way to the far end, 100 feet away. The near one looks big and bright and makes you squint. The far one is a small dot. Both bulbs are putting out the same light.
look.prompt: How is this like the sun and the night stars? What would you need to know to tell whether a dim star is actually small, or just far away?

check.q: What is the sun?
choices: A giant ball of burning wood
A star that makes its own light
check.why: The sun is a star: a huge ball of hot gas that produces its own light and heat.

check.q: Why does the sun look so much bigger and brighter than other stars?
choices: It is the biggest star in the universe
It is the only star that gives off light
It is made of different stuff
It is much closer to Earth
check.why: The sun is a normal-sized star, but it is millions of times closer than any other star.

check.q: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. What does that tell you?
choices: The sun is very far away even though light is very fast
The sun turns off every 8 minutes
check.why: Light is the fastest thing known, so an 8-minute trip means an enormous distance.

lessons.title: Why Stars Look Different
lessons.mainIdea: Stars look brighter or dimmer mostly because of how far away they are, and their distances are enormous.
reading: Look up on a clear night. Some stars are bright. Some you can barely see. Two things decide that. One is how much light the star really gives off. The other is distance. A bright star far away can look dimmer than a weak star nearby.

Star distances are so big that miles stop being useful. Astronomers use the *light-year*, the distance light travels in one year. That is about 6 trillion miles. The nearest star after the sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4 light-years away. Its light left it four years ago.

Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is about 8.6 light-years away. Some stars you can see are hundreds of light-years off. Their light left them before your grandparents were born. Looking at stars is looking back in time.

words.d: the distance light travels in one year, about 6 trillion miles
a scientist who studies stars, planets and space

look.title: How Far Is Far?
look.prompt: Sirius looks brighter than Proxima Centauri even though it is twice as far away. What must be true about Sirius?

check.q: What is a light-year?
choices: The time it takes Earth to circle the sun
One year on a distant planet
The distance light travels in one year
check.why: A light-year measures distance, not time: how far light goes in a year.

check.q: Two stars give off the same amount of light. One is 10 light-years away and one is 100. Which looks brighter?
check.why: The closer star looks brighter, just like the near flashlight in the hall.

check.q: You see a star 100 light-years away. When did the light you see leave it?
check.why: Light took 100 years to cross 100 light-years, so you are seeing the star as it was 100 years ago.

lessons.title: Patterns in the Night Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Stars form patterns that stay the same night after night, so people have used them as a map.
reading: Stars do not move around compared to each other. The same groups appear in the same shapes year after year. People long ago connected them into pictures and gave them names. Those groups are *constellations*. The Big Dipper, with its seven bright stars, is one part of a larger one.

The Big Dipper is a good starting point in Illinois. It can be seen on any clear night of the year. Follow the two stars at the end of its bowl and you reach Polaris, the North Star. Polaris sits almost straight above Earth's North Pole, so it always marks north.

Sailors and travelers steered by Polaris for centuries. Before compasses, before maps, the stars were the map. Once you learn a few constellations, the night sky stops being random dots. It becomes a place with landmarks, and you can find your way in it.

words.d: a group of stars that people see as a pattern or picture
the North Star; it sits almost above Earth's North Pole and always marks north

look.title: Lost in the Dark
look.text: A camper in downstate Illinois walks away from the tent at night and loses the trail. There is no phone signal. The sky is clear. She remembers that the tent is north of the road. She finds the Big Dipper and follows the two stars at the end of its bowl to a medium-bright star that does not seem to move.
look.prompt: How can she use that star to walk back toward the road, and why does it work no matter what time of night it is?

check.q: What is a constellation?
choices: A star that moves across the sky
A group of stars seen as a pattern
check.why: Constellations are star groups that people connect into shapes and name.

check.q: Why does Polaris always show north?
choices: It sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole
It rises in the north every evening
check.why: Because it lies above the pole Earth spins around, it barely moves as Earth turns.

check.q: Why are the constellations the same shape every year?
choices: Stars are so far away that their motion is too small to notice
The sky is a painted dome
check.why: Stars do move, but they are so distant that the patterns look fixed for thousands of years.

lessons.title: Earth Spins
lessons.mainIdea: Earth rotates once every 24 hours, and that spin is what makes day and night.
reading: Earth is a ball spinning in space. It turns all the way around once every 24 hours. That spin is called *rotation*. Earth rotates around an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, its *axis*. You cannot feel the spin because everything around you spins with you.

Half of Earth always faces the sun. That half has day. The other half faces away, into dark space. That half has night. As Earth turns, your town swings from the dark side into the lit side. That is sunrise. Later it swings back into the dark. That is sunset.

It is tempting to say the sun goes around Earth. It looks that way. But if the sun moved and Earth sat still, the stars would have to circle us every day too, and so would the moon, all at the same speed. One spinning Earth explains everything at once. That is why scientists trust it.

words.d: spinning around a center line, the way a top spins
the imaginary line through the North and South Poles that Earth spins around

look.title: The Lamp and the Orange
look.text: In a dark room, a lamp stands for the sun. A student holds an orange with a pin stuck in it for Chicago. She turns the orange slowly. The pin comes into the light: morning. It faces the lamp straight on: noon. It slides into shadow: evening. It spends a while in the dark, then comes back into the light.
look.prompt: In this model, what does one full turn of the orange stand for? What would you have to change to make Chicago's day longer?

check.q: What causes day and night?
choices: The sun turning on and off
check.why: As Earth rotates, each place turns into the sunlight and then away from it.

check.q: How long does one full rotation of Earth take?
check.why: One spin takes about 24 hours, which is one day.

check.q: Why can't you feel Earth spinning?
choices: Earth spins too slowly to matter
The spin only happens at night
Everything around you is spinning along with you
check.why: The ground, the air and you all move together, so nothing seems to move.

lessons.title: The Sun's Daily Path
lessons.mainIdea: Because Earth spins, the sun appears to rise in the east, climb high toward the south, and set in the west.
reading: Earth spins toward the east. So the sun seems to come up in the east. It climbs higher through the morning. In Illinois, it is never straight overhead. At *noon* it is highest, and it stands in the southern half of the sky. Then it sinks and sets in the west.

That path is why south-facing windows get the most sun. It is why a sidewalk on the north side of a building stays icy longest. It is why the noon shadow of a stick points north. The sun is to the south, so the shadow falls the other way.

The path changes a little with the seasons. In summer the sun rises in the northeast and climbs very high. In winter it rises in the southeast and stays low. But east to west, low to high to low, is the same every single day. It is one of the most reliable patterns on Earth.

words.d: the middle of the day, when the sun is highest in the sky
the line where the sky seems to meet the ground

look.title: The Icy Sidewalk
look.text: A week after a snowstorm, the sidewalk on the south side of the school is dry. The sidewalk on the north side, right against the building, is still a sheet of ice. Both got the same snow. The custodian salted both. The building is three stories tall.
look.prompt: Why did the south side melt first? Where is the sun during the school day, and what does the building do to the north side?

check.q: Where does the sun appear to rise?
check.why: Earth spins toward the east, so the sun first appears on the eastern horizon.

check.q: At noon in Illinois, where is the sun?
check.why: From Illinois the noon sun is high but always in the southern half of the sky.

check.q: A stick's shadow at noon points north. What does that tell you about the sun?
choices: The sun is to the south
The sun is to the north
check.why: Shadows fall away from the light, so a north-pointing shadow means the sun is in the south.

lessons.title: Shadows Through the Day
lessons.mainIdea: A shadow's length and direction change through the day in a pattern that tracks the sun's path.
reading: A *shadow* is the dark spot where something blocks the light. Your shadow stretches away from the sun. When the sun is low, near the horizon, shadows are long. When the sun is high, shadows are short. That is the whole rule, and it makes a shadow a clock.

In the morning the sun is low in the east. Shadows are long and point west. By noon the sun is high in the south. Shadows are short and point north. In the afternoon the sun sinks toward the west. Shadows grow long again, pointing east.

People used this for thousands of years. A *sundial* is just a stick and a set of marks. Record the shadow every hour for one day. Then the marks tell time on any sunny day. You can also check the pattern. It repeats, day after day, with tiny changes through the year.

words.d: the dark area behind something that blocks light
a clock made from a stick and marks; the stick's shadow points to the time

look.title: The Shadow Stick Log
look.unit: inches, shadow length of a 24-inch stick
look.cite: a class record on a spring day in Illinois, rounded
look.prompt: When was the shadow shortest? Why is the 1 p.m. shadow still almost as long as the stick, even at the sun's highest point?

check.q: When are shadows shortest?
choices: When the sun is low in the sky
When the sun is highest in the sky
check.why: A high sun makes light come down steeply, so the shadow is short.

check.q: In the morning, a stick's shadow points west. Where is the sun?
check.why: Shadows point away from the light, so a west-pointing shadow means the sun is in the east.

check.q: How can a shadow work like a clock?
choices: The shadow's direction and length change in a repeating daily pattern
Shadows always point at the time
Shadows only appear at certain times
check.why: Because the sun's path repeats each day, the shadow at each hour lands in the same place.

sections.title: The Year, the Moon and Gravity

lessons.title: Why We Have Seasons
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's tilt, not its distance from the sun, causes the seasons by changing how directly sunlight hits us.
reading: Earth travels around the sun once a year. That trip is its *orbit*. Earth's axis is tilted, about 23.5 degrees, and the tilt always points the same way in space. For part of the year the northern half leans toward the sun. For the other part it leans away.

When Illinois leans toward the sun, the sun climbs high and days are long. Sunlight hits the ground more directly and heats it more. That is summer. Chicago gets about 15 hours of daylight in late June. When Illinois leans away, the sun stays low and days are short, about 9 hours in late December. That is winter.

Many people think summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun. It is not true. Earth is actually a little closer to the sun in January. The *tilt* is what matters. That is also why Australia has summer while Illinois has winter. The southern half is leaning toward the sun then.

words.d: the path one object takes around another, like Earth around the sun
a lean to one side; Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees
hitting straight on rather than at a slant

look.title: The Flashlight on the Table
look.text: Shine a flashlight straight down on a table. It makes a small, bright circle. Now tilt the flashlight so the beam hits at a slant. The same light spreads into a long, dim oval. The flashlight did not change. The bulb is the same distance away. Only the angle changed.
look.prompt: Which patch of table would warm up more? How does this explain why winter sunlight, low and slanting, feels weak?

check.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
choices: Earth's distance from the sun changing
The sun getting hotter and cooler
The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the sun
check.why: The tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each half of Earth through the year.

check.q: When it is summer in Illinois, what season is it in Australia?
check.why: The southern half leans away from the sun when the northern half leans toward it.

check.q: Earth is slightly closer to the sun in January. Why isn't January warm in Illinois?
choices: The small distance change matters less than the tilt
The sun is dimmer in January
Earth is not really closer in January
check.why: The tilt makes January sunlight slanted and weak, which outweighs the small change in distance.

lessons.title: Stars of the Seasons
lessons.mainIdea: As Earth moves around the sun, the night side faces different directions, so different stars appear each season.
reading: Orion, the hunter with three stars in a row for a belt, rules the winter sky in Illinois. By July, it is gone. In its place, near the southern horizon, the curled tail of Scorpius appears. Then Orion comes back in December. The stars did not move. Earth did.

Night is the side of Earth facing away from the sun. As Earth goes around its orbit, that dark side points at a different part of space each season. In winter it points toward Orion. In summer it points the other way, toward Scorpius. Orion is still there in summer, but it is up during the day, lost in sunlight.

Some stars never leave. The Big Dipper and Polaris sit near the direction of Earth's axis. So they are visible all year from Illinois. Watching which constellations come and go is another pattern. This one takes a whole year to repeat.

words.d: a winter constellation with three bright stars in a row for a belt
changing with the seasons, repeating once a year

look.title: The Campfire Circle
look.text: Picture a campfire in the middle of a big field with a barn on one side and a pond on the other. You walk slowly in a circle around the fire, always facing away from it. When you are on the barn side, you see the pond. When you reach the pond side, you see the barn. You never see whatever is behind the fire.
look.prompt: What stands for the sun, Earth and the stars in this picture? Why can't you see 'summer stars' in winter?

check.q: Why can you see Orion in winter but not in summer?
choices: Orion moves to the other side of the sky
Earth's night side faces a different direction in each season
check.why: As Earth orbits, the dark side points at different stars; in summer Orion is up in daytime.

check.q: Which stars can be seen from Illinois all year?
check.why: Stars near the direction of Earth's axis, like Polaris, stay in view all year.

check.q: How long does the pattern of seasonal constellations take to repeat?
check.why: It follows Earth's orbit, which takes one year.

lessons.title: The Moon's Changing Face
lessons.mainIdea: The moon's phases repeat about every 29.5 days as we see different amounts of its sunlit half.
reading: The moon does not make its own light. It reflects sunlight. Half of the moon is always lit by the sun, just as half of Earth is. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see. The shapes we see are the *phases* of the moon.

The moon orbits Earth about once a month. When it is between Earth and the sun, its lit side faces away from us. We see nothing: a new moon. A week later we see half of it: first quarter. Two weeks in, the whole lit side faces us: full moon. Then it shrinks back.

The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days. In 1610, Galileo pointed one of the first telescopes at the moon. He saw mountains and craters, not a smooth glowing disk. He measured the mountains from their shadows. The moon was a world, with ground you could stand on.

words.d: the shape of the lit part of the moon that we see from Earth
a bowl-shaped hole made when a rock from space hits a surface
to bounce light back rather than make it

look.title: Galileo Looks at the Moon
look.text: In 1610 Galileo reported that the moon is not smooth and polished, as people had believed, but rough and uneven, full of hollows and bumps like the face of Earth itself, with mountain ranges and deep valleys. He worked out the height of lunar mountains from the length of their shadows near the line between light and dark.
look.prompt: Galileo used shadows to measure mountains on the moon. How is that like the shadow stick on the blacktop?

check.q: Where does the moon's light come from?
choices: The moon makes its own light
It reflects light from Earth's cities
check.why: The moon is rock. We see it because sunlight bounces off it.

check.q: About how long does it take the moon to go through all its phases?
check.why: The full cycle from new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.

check.q: What did Galileo discover about the moon in 1610?
check.why: Through his telescope Galileo saw shadows of mountains and craters on the moon's surface.

lessons.title: Down Means Toward the Center
lessons.mainIdea: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth's center, which is why 'down' points the same way everywhere on Earth.
reading: Drop a ball. It falls. Drop it in Chicago, in Australia, or at the South Pole. It falls toward the ground every time. *Gravity* is the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth. On a round planet, 'down' means toward the middle, wherever you stand.

That is why people in Australia do not fall off. Their 'down' points toward Earth's center too, just like yours. Gravity also holds the air close to Earth and keeps the moon circling us. It is the same pull, everywhere, all the time.

In July 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts landed on the moon. The moon's gravity is about one sixth as strong as Earth's, so they bounced in slow hops. But they did not float away. The moon pulled them toward its center, just as Earth pulls you. Gravity works on every world.

words.d: the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth or another large object
the middle point of something

look.title: The Eagle Has Landed
look.text: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.
look.cite: Neil Armstrong, Apollo 11 radio transmission to Mission Control, July 20, 1969 (NASA)
look.prompt: The lander had to fire its engine to slow down before touching the moon. What would have happened if the moon had no gravity at all?

check.q: Which way does gravity pull you?
check.why: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth's center, so 'down' means toward the middle.

check.q: Why don't people in Australia fall off Earth?
choices: Gravity pulls them toward Earth's center too
Australia is on top of Earth
check.why: Gravity points toward the center everywhere, so their down is toward the ground under them.

check.q: On the moon, astronauts bounced in slow hops. What does that show?
choices: The moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's but still pulls down
Earth's gravity reached them on the moon
check.why: The moon's pull is about one sixth of Earth's, so astronauts could hop high but still came down.

review.q: Why does the sun look so much bigger than other stars?
choices: It is the largest star known
It is far closer to Earth
It is the only true star
review.why: The sun is an ordinary star; it is enormous in our sky only because it is so near.
As Earth spins, each place turns into sunlight and back into darkness.

review.q: At noon in Illinois, a stick's shadow is
review.why: The noon sun is high in the south, so the shadow is short and falls to the north.

choices: Earth's changing distance from the sun
review.why: The tilt changes how directly sunlight strikes each hemisphere through the year.

review.q: Why does Orion appear in winter but not in summer?
choices: It moves to the other side of the sky
Earth's night side faces a different direction each season
It is hidden by the moon
review.why: As Earth orbits, the dark side points at different stars; in summer Orion is up by day.

review.q: About how long is the cycle of the moon's phases?
review.why: From new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days, roughly a month.

review.q: A star is 25 light-years away. What does that mean?
choices: Its light takes 25 years to reach us
It will burn out in 25 years
review.why: A light-year is distance; light from that star traveled 25 years to reach your eye.

review.q: Which sentence about gravity is correct?
choices: It pulls toward Earth's center from everywhere on Earth
It pushes things away from the ground
review.why: Gravity pulls everything toward the center; that is why down is toward the ground anywhere on Earth.
